mainTopic: Buying in another's name, רב כהנא's flax and ריבית, and the new משנה on returning stolen money after a false oath
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא about someone who buys a field in another person's name. The seller does not have to write the real buyer a second שטר unless the buyer made it a condition (על מנת). The גמרא asks why each half of the ברייתא is needed and gives a 'you might have thought' answer for each. Then comes a story: רב כהנא paid in advance for flax, the price went up, and the seller sold it. רב tells him he may take the money only if the flax was sold as רב כהנא's. The גמרא first wonders whether this follows only בני מערבא, then rejects that idea. It explains instead that this was only a trust deal (אמנה), and רב allows trust deals in produce but not in money. Finally a new משנה begins. A robber who swore falsely must bring the payment to the victim himself, even as far as מדי, if at least a פרוטה of the קרן is still owed. The amud ends as the משנה starts a new case about a false oath over the חומש, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ruling: no second sale, unless there was a condition
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends: the seller is not forced to 'sell again' (write a new שטר in the real buyer's name), unless the buyer stipulated 'on condition'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The seller is not forced to sell the field a second time. But if the buyer said 'on condition that you give me a שטר in my name,' the seller is forced to sell again.
steps.whatsHappening: We are hearing the last lines of a ברייתא about someone who bought a field using another person's name. It tells us when the seller must write a new שטר for the real buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Selling another time' here means writing a new שטר that names the real buyer as owner. Normally the seller does not have to do this. If the buyer set it as an explicit condition of the deal, the seller must.

keyTerms.meaning: On condition that, an explicit stipulation

phrases.english: The seller is not compelled
to sell another time.
phrases.notes: 'Selling again' means writing a new שטר that names the real buyer as the owner.

phrases.english: But if he said to him: 'on condition'
the seller is compelled to sell.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין כּוֹפִין אֶת הַמּוֹכֵר לִמְכּוֹר זִימְנָא אַחֲרִיתִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes the ברייתא that began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without an explicit condition, the seller need not write a new שטר for the real buyer. With 'על מנת', he must.

steps.title: Isn't the first ruling obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the first half of the ברייתא and asks: why would we need to be told this?
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: someone who buys a field in his friend's name, the seller is not forced to sell again. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first half of the ברייתא and challenges it: this seems too obvious to need saying. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer himself chose to put the deal in another person's name. So of course the seller owes him nothing more. The גמרא wants to know what new point the ברייתא is teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said, used to quote an earlier source
It's obvious! (a challenge that a teaching is unnecessary)

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: 'The Master' here is the ברייתא we just finished.

phrases.english: One who buys a field in his friend's name
the seller is not compelled
to sell another time.
Isn't it obvious?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Re-quotes the first clause of the ברייתא in order to question why it is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first clause of the ברייתא (no second sale).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since the buyer chose another person's name himself, the ruling seems self-evident and not worth stating.

steps.title: You might have thought the buyer could claim he paid only for his own benefit
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is needed because the buyer could argue the seller knew the purchase was really for him. It teaches that the seller can answer: I made the deal with the man whose name you used, so get your שטר from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think the buyer can say: 'You knew I was buying for myself. I only used his name as protection. I don't throw money away for nothing, so I paid expecting you to write me another שטר.' The ברייתא teaches that the seller can answer: 'I did business with the person whose name you bought in. Let him write you another שטר.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a 'you might have thought' argument. It shows a reasonable claim the buyer could make, then explains why the ברייתא rejects it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer's claim sounds strong: everyone knew the field was really his, and the other name was only a shield. Even so, the seller's only legal deal was with the named person. So the real buyer must turn to that person for a new שטר, not to the seller.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said, introduces a mistaken assumption

phrases.english: You might have said that he can say to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the real buyer, speaking to the seller.

phrases.english: You surely knew
that I was taking it for myself
and it was merely protection that I wanted
and I don't throw away my money for nothing

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אַדַּעְתָּא דְּכָתֵב לֵיהּ שְׁטָרָא אַחֲרִינָא;
phrases.english: rather, it was with the understanding that you would write another document
It teaches us that he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Now 'he' is the seller, answering the buyer.

phrases.english: I did a deal for you
with that person in whose name you bought it
so let him write you another document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge by showing a non-obvious claim the ברייתא rules out.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: shows a plausible mistaken assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer could force the seller to write a new שטר, since the seller knew the field was really for him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The seller dealt with the named person, and the buyer must get his שטר from that person.
steps.whatToRemember: When you buy in someone else's name, your legal partner is that named person. Without a stated condition, the seller owes you nothing more.

steps.title: Isn't the 'on condition' ruling obvious too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the second half of the ברייתא and again asks why it needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he said 'on condition', the seller is forced to sell. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the second half of the ברייתא and asks the same question: isn't this obvious? This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the buyer explicitly made a new שטר a condition of the deal, the seller clearly has to keep the condition. So what is the ברייתא adding?

phrases.english: And if he said to him 'on condition'
the seller is compelled to sell.
Isn't it obvious?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אָמַר לוֹ עַל מְנָת כּוֹפִין אֶת הַמּוֹכֵר לִמְכּוֹר פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question as Step 2, now aimed at the second clause of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second clause of the ברייתא (על מנת forces a sale).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An explicit condition clearly binds the seller, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The case is where the buyer told the witnesses in front of the seller
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed for a case where the buyer told witnesses, while the seller was present, 'I want another שטר.' The seller cannot claim he thought the buyer meant a שטר from the named person.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed where the buyer said to the witnesses, in front of the seller: 'See that I want another שטר.' You might think the seller can say: 'I thought you meant a שטר from the person in whose name you bought.' The ברייתא teaches that the buyer can answer: 'That is exactly why I bothered to tell the witnesses in front of you. I want it from you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the 'on condition' case is not the simple one. It is a case where the buyer's request was vague, and the seller could try to claim he misunderstood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the buyer never spelled out who should write the second שטר, so the seller might claim he thought it meant the named person. The ברייתא rules that saying it to the witnesses in the seller's presence shows it was aimed at the seller. So the seller is bound.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a specific case)

phrases.english: No, it is needed where he said to the witnesses
in front of him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the seller, who was standing right there.

phrases.english: See that I want another document.
You might have said that he can say to him:
I thought, a document from that one
in whose name you bought, is what you were talking about
It teaches us that he can say to him:
For this reason I bothered and said
to the witnesses in front of you
that it is from you that I want it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דַּאֲמַר לְהוּ לְסָהֲדִי קַמֵּיהּ דִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second פשיטא by narrowing the case to a vague request made before witnesses.
steps.terutzResolutionType: לא צריכא: limits the ruling to a specific, less obvious case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The seller could claim he understood the request as aimed at the named person.
steps.terutzMaskana: Speaking to the witnesses in the seller's presence shows the request was aimed at the seller, so he is forced to write the שטר.
steps.whatToRemember: Both halves of the ברייתא teach something new. The real buyer cannot force the seller just because the seller knew the truth. But a request made openly in front of the seller, before witnesses, does bind him.

steps.title: רב כהנא's flax: may he take the money?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא paid in advance for flax. The flax rose in price, and its owner sold it. רב כהנא asks רב whether he may take the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא gave money for flax. In the end, the flax went up in price, and the owner of the flax sold it. רב כהנא came before רב and said: 'What should I do? Should I go take my money?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related story about buying something through another person. רב כהנא asks רב a practical question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא paid but left the flax with the seller. When the seller sold it at a higher price, רב כהנא would get back more than he paid. This could look like a loan repaid with extra, which is רבית.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana gave money for flax.
In the end, the flax went up in price,
and the owner of the flax sold it.
He came before Rav and said to him:
What should I do? Should I go take my money?
phrases.notes: He is asking whether taking the money, which is now more than he paid, is allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story on the related theme of whose name a sale is made in.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: May רב כהנא collect the proceeds of the flax sale, which are more than he paid?

steps.title: רב: it depends whether the flax was sold as רב כהנא's
steps.stepSummary: רב rules: if the sellers said 'this flax is כהנא's' when selling it, take the money. If not, don't take it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to him: 'If, when they were selling it, they said, "This flax is כהנא's," go take the money. And if not, don't take it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers with a condition. Everything depends on whose name the flax was sold in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the flax was sold as רב כהנא's, the sale was really his own, so the profit is his. If it was not, the seller sold his own flax, and the extra money would look like a loan paid back with רבית.

keyTerms.meaning: Interest, forbidden extra payment on a loan

steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying the money is always forbidden or always allowed. The deciding detail is whether the flax was sold in רב כהנא's name.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ties back to the ברייתא's theme: whose name a sale is made in decides who the real party to it is.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי כִּי קָא [מְ]זַבְּנִי אָמְרִי:
phrases.english: He said to him: If, when they were selling it, they said:
phrases.notes: Some versions add the letter in square brackets; it doesn't change the meaning.

phrases.english: 'This flax is Kahana's,'
go take it;
and if not, do not take it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי כִּי קָא מְזַבְּנִי אָמְרִי
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Take the money only if the flax was sold explicitly as רב כהנא's. Otherwise, do not, because of the concern of רבית.
steps.whatToRemember: A sale made in my name is my sale, and its profit is mine. Profit from a sale made in the seller's own name can look like רבית.

steps.title: Does רב's ruling follow only the people of the West?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רב's ruling about the flax follows only the view of בני מערבא, who hold that a sale counts for someone else only if the seller says so openly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is רב following? Is it only the view of the people of ארץ ישראל, who say: Who told the wheat owner that he should give the wheat to the owner of the money?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which earlier opinion רב's ruling depends on. It suggests that the ruling fits only the view of בני מערבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the previous amud, בני מערבא held that a seller passes ownership to someone else only if he says so openly. If so, when the flax seller did not say 'this is כהנא's', the money is his own, and giving it to רב כהנא would look like ריבית. The suggestion is that רב's 'if not, don't take it' depends on this one view.

keyTerms.meaning: In accordance with whom? The גמרא is asking whose opinion a ruling follows
The people of the West, meaning the Sages of ארץ ישראל
The owner of the wheat, here the seller
The owner of the money, the one who paid

phrases.english: In accordance with whom?
phrases.notes: He means: whose opinion is רב following in his ruling to רב כהנא?

phrases.english: Like the people of the West, who say:
phrases.notes: 'The West' means ארץ ישראל. This line was quoted earlier in this discussion, on the previous amud.

phrases.english: Who informed the owner of the wheat
that he should transfer the wheat to the owner of the money?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what view underlies רב's ruling from Step 7
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב's ruling depends only on the view of בני מערבא, that a sale counts for another person only when stated openly

steps.title: רב כהנא did not lend money; the seller robbed him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. רב כהנא did not lend money and get back more. The flax rose in value by itself, and selling it was robbery, so the seller must pay its full value anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say רב כהנא gave four and took back eight? The flax went up in price on its own. They robbed him of it, and we learned: all robbers pay according to the value at the time of the robbery!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the idea from Step 8. It says there is no ריבית question here at all, because this was robbery, not a loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריבית means getting paid extra for lending money, but רב כהנא lent nothing. He bought flax, it went up in value by itself, and the seller who sold it stole רב כהנא's flax. A גזלן pays the value at the time of the robbery, which was the higher price, so רב כהנא should be able to take the money no matter whose view we follow.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? Used to reject an assumption

steps.confusionAlert: 'Four' and 'eight' are just example numbers. The point is that רב כהנא did not lend four and get eight back, so this is not ריבית.

phrases.aramaic: אַטּוּ מִי יָהֵיב רַב כָּהֲנָא אַרְבַּע,
phrases.english: Is that to say Rav Kahana gave four
and took eight?!
phrases.notes: He means it was not a loan with extra paid back, which would be ריבית.

phrases.english: It is the flax that rose in price by itself;
they actually robbed him of it,
and we learned in a mishna:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה on 93b of this מסכת.

phrases.english: All robbers pay according to the time of the robbery!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ מִי יָהֵיב רַב כָּהֲנָא אַרְבַּע, וְשָׁקֵיל תַּמְנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the explanation offered in Step 8
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole idea that רב's ruling depends on בני מערבא and a ריבית concern
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: If the flax belonged to רב כהנא, there was no loan. Selling it was robbery, and a robber pays the value at the time of the robbery, so taking the money is allowed under every view.

steps.title: It was only a trust deal, and רב allows trust only in produce
steps.stepSummary: The real case: רב כהנא never made a formal acquisition of the flax, so it was only a trust deal (אמנה). רב holds that a trust deal may be settled in produce but not in money.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: There it was a trust deal, and רב כהנא never pulled the flax to acquire it. And רב follows his own reasoning, as רב said: One may make a trust deal for produce, but not a trust deal for money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new explanation of רב's ruling. The flax never became רב כהנא's, and רב has a known rule about advance-payment deals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא paid in advance but never did משיכה, so the flax still belonged to the seller. That means there was no robbery, only a trust deal. רב holds that someone who paid in advance may later receive produce, but may not receive cash worth more than he paid, because that looks like ריבית. If the sellers said 'this flax is כהנא's', it counts as selling his flax for him, so he may take the money. If not, he would only be getting extra cash, which is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A trust deal: paying in advance and trusting the seller to deliver later
Pulling an item, the act that formally acquires movable goods

steps.whatToRemember: רב's ruling rests on his own rule: an advance payment without משיכה is only a trust deal. It may be paid back in produce but not in money. So רב כהנא may take the money only if the sellers openly sold the flax as his.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a practical rule for advance purchases: the buyer may receive the goods later, but not their higher cash value, because that looks like ריבית.

phrases.english: They say:
There it was a matter of trust,
phrases.notes: 'Trust' here means he paid in advance and simply trusted the seller to hand over the flax later.

phrases.english: and Rav Kahana did not pull the flax;
phrases.notes: Pulling is how you formally acquire movable things. Without it, the flax was still the seller's.

phrases.english: and Rav follows his own reasoning,
as Rav said:
One may make a trust arrangement with produce,
but one may not make a trust arrangement with money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty raised in Step 9 by redefining the case
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (no משיכה, so no robbery) plus רב's own known rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the flax was already רב כהנא's, so selling it was robbery and the money is plainly his.
steps.terutzMaskana: The flax was never acquired, so it was only a trust deal. רב allows trust deals in produce but not in money, which explains his two-sided ruling.

steps.title: New משנה: a robber who swore falsely must return the payment to the victim himself
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: someone who robbed a פרוטה's worth and swore falsely must bring the payment to the victim himself, even as far as מדי. He may not give it to the victim's son or agent, but he may give it to a שליח בית דין. If the victim died, he gives it to the heirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who robs his fellow of something worth a פרוטה and swears to him falsely must bring it after him, even to מדי. He may not give it to his son or to his agent, but he may give it to an agent of the court. If the victim died, he returns it to his heirs.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new topic. It explains how a robber who lied under oath must return what he stole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because this robber swore falsely, he cannot repair what he did until the payment actually reaches the victim. So he must chase the victim, even to a far-off land like מדי. Giving it to the victim's son or the victim's own agent is not enough, but a שליח בית דין is acceptable, and after the victim's death the heirs receive it.

keyTerms.meaning: Worth a פרוטה, the smallest amount of money that counts
Swore, here a false oath denying the robbery
An agent appointed by the court

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who robs another of something worth a peruta,
and swears to him,
phrases.notes: He swore falsely that he did not rob, and now he wants to do תשובה and pay back.

phrases.english: must bring it after him, even to Media.
He may not give it to his son,
and not to his agent,
but he may give it to an agent of the court.
And if he died, he returns it to his heirs.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַגּוֹזֵל אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה, וְנִשְׁבַּע לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A robber who swore falsely must bring the payment to the victim himself, even to a distant place. A son or the victim's own agent is not enough, but a court agent is, and after death the heirs receive it.

steps.title: Cases where the robber does not need to go after the victim
steps.stepSummary: If what is still owed is only the חומש, or less than a פרוטה's worth of the קרן, the robber does not need to travel after the victim.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he gave the victim the original value but not the extra fifth, or the victim forgave the original value but not the extra fifth, or the victim forgave both except for less than a פרוטה of the original value, the robber does not need to go after him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה lists three cases where the robber does not have to travel after the victim to pay what is left.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 11 the robber had to bring the payment himself, even as far as מדי. That strict rule applies only to the קרן worth a פרוטה or more. When the only thing left is the חומש, or a tiny leftover of the קרן below a פרוטה, he does not need to travel. Where the חומש is still owed, he still has to pay it, but he does not have to chase the victim to do so.

keyTerms.meaning: The principal: the original value of what was stolen
The extra fifth a robber who swore falsely must add
Less than a פרוטה's worth, too small to count as real money in halacha
To go after him, meaning to travel to the victim to pay

steps.confusionAlert: "He does not need to go after him" does not mean an unpaid חומש is cancelled. It only means he does not have to travel to pay it.

phrases.english: If he gave him the principal,
but did not give him the fifth;
phrases.notes: The fifth is the extra payment added on top of the stolen value, because he swore falsely.

phrases.english: or he forgave him the principal,
but did not forgive him the fifth;

phrases.aramaic: מָחַל לוֹ עַל זֶה וְעַל זֶה,
phrases.english: or he forgave him both this and that,
phrases.notes: "This and that" means both the principal and the fifth.

phrases.english: except for less than a peruta's worth of the principal,
he does not need to go after him.
phrases.notes: Going after him is the travel from step 11, "even as far as מדי."

steps.triggerLanguage: נָתַן לוֹ אֶת הַקֶּרֶן, וְלֹא נָתַן לוֹ אֶת הַחוֹמֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the travel rule from step 11 by listing cases where it does not apply.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If only the חומש, or less than a פרוטה of the קרן, is still owed, the robber need not travel after the victim.

steps.title: Cases where the robber must go after the victim
steps.stepSummary: If a פרוטה or more of the קרן is still owed, the robber must travel after the victim, even if the חומש was paid or forgiven.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he gave the extra fifth but not the original value, or the victim forgave the extra fifth but not the original value, or the victim forgave both except for a פרוטה's worth of the original value, the robber must go after him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the three opposite cases, where the robber must travel after the victim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These cases mirror step 12, but now the missing part is the קרן, and it is worth at least a פרוטה. The point is that the travel rule depends on the קרן. Even a single פרוטה of קרן still owed means he must go to the victim.

keyTerms.meaning: Worth a פרוטה, the smallest amount that counts as money in halacha

steps.whatToRemember: The travel requirement depends on the קרן. A פרוטה or more of קרן still owed means he must travel. If only the חומש or less than a פרוטה is left, he does not.

phrases.english: If he gave him the fifth,
but did not give him the principal;
or he forgave him the fifth,
but did not forgive him the principal;

phrases.aramaic: מָחַל לוֹ עַל זֶה וְעַל זֶה,
phrases.english: or he forgave him both this and that,
except for a peruta's worth of the principal,
he must go after him.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָתַן לוֹ אֶת הַחוֹמֶשׁ, וְלֹא נָתַן לוֹ אֶת הַקֶּרֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite cases to step 12, where the travel rule does apply.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a פרוטה or more of the קרן is still owed, the robber must travel after the victim.

steps.title: New case: he paid the principal and swore falsely about the fifth
steps.stepSummary: The משנה starts a new case: the robber paid the קרן and then swore falsely that he had already paid the חומש.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he gave him the original value and then swore to him about the extra fifth...
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is setting up its next case. Here we only get the facts, and the ruling comes in the lines that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the false oath was about the stolen item itself. Here the robber already paid the קרן but lies under oath about the חומש. The question this sets up is how a second false oath about the חומש changes what he owes.

keyTerms.meaning: Swore an oath, here a false one

phrases.english: If he gave him the principal,
and swore to him about the fifth,
phrases.notes: He falsely swore he had already paid the fifth. The ruling comes in the next lines.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָתַן לוֹ אֶת הַקֶּרֶן, וְנִשְׁבַּע לוֹ עַל הַחוֹמֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the travel rule to a new case of a false oath about the חומש itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Facts only so far: the קרן was paid, and a false oath was made about the חומש. The ruling follows.
